land.text: Novgorod, which Yaroslav's division of 1054 gave to Iziaslav I with Kiev (Kievan Rus' page); Cliopatria's first shape of this state is 1056

predecessors.note: The Novgorod page dates the republic from 1136 (infobox 'Established 1136'); before that Novgorod was a Rus' principality under princes sent from Kiev. Cliopatria draws one continuous 'Novgorod Republic' shape from 1056, so one dossier carries both phases and the 1136 change is a rename event.

land.text: the whole Novgorod land as it stood in 1468, annexed by Ivan III in January 1478 ('Novgorod was then formally annexed by Moscow in 1478', Battle of Shelon page)

successors.note: Cliopatria instead gives Moscow the northern 5,900 cells from 1475 and keeps a Novgorod core of 658 cells to 1481; the pages date the annexation to January 1478 (see keyframe novgorod-republic_1475).

capitals.name: Novgorod (Veliky Novgorod)
capitals.note: Novgorod page infobox: capital Novgorod (Veliky Novgorod); the princes' residences at Yaroslav's Court and Rurikovo Gorodishche were not capitals.

correction.text: the Novgorod land of the 1056 shape, held from 1054 as part of the principality of Kiev and Novgorod under Iziaslav I

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's first Novgorod shape begins in 1056, but the Kievan Rus' page makes Yaroslav's division 'after the death of Yaroslav I in 1054' ('Principality of Kiev and Novgorod, for the eldest son Iziaslav I of Kiev'), and the rus dossier hands the land over in 1054. The 1056 shape is used for 1054-1055.

378,000 km2 around Lake Ilmen, Lake Ladoga and the upper Volga-Onega divide, to 64.5 N. The infobox of the Novgorod page gives no area (it calls the republic 'the largest of the Russian states in terms of area' before Moscow), so nothing to compare. The Kievan Rus' page gives Novgorod to Iziaslav I in 1054; the Council of Liubech page (1097) gives 'Great Novgorod' to Monomakh's son Mstislav.

378,900 km2: the 1056 shape plus one cell at 65.1 N. The Novgorod page has the Novgorodians trading with the Yugra tribes by 1096 and going 'beyond the portage' and to Pomorye in 1079, but dates no frontier.
379,000 km2, unchanged but for one cell. The page records 'Novgorod paid tribute to the grand prince of Kiev' in 1113; no frontier change.

542,300 km2: +693 cells (about 163,000 km2) to 44.7 E and 65.1 N, the Vaga-Sukhona-Dvina side of the portage. No page gives the year 1126; the Pomors page says 'As early as the 12th century, explorers from Novgorod entered the White Sea through the Northern Dvina' and 'In the 12th-15th centuries, Pomorye was considered an extensive colony of' Novgorod, and the Novgorod page has the 1079 journey 'beyond the portage'. Kept; the ledger gain at 1126 is confidence 1.
Same shape as 1126. The page: 'Established 1136': in 1136 the Novgorodians deposed Vsevolod Mstislavich and began electing and dismissing princes; a rename event, not a border change.
Same shape (one cell more). Page: 1156 Novgorod wins the right to choose its bishop, 1165 the bishopric becomes an archbishopric; no frontier change.
Same shape (one cell fewer). No frontier event on the page for 1202.

Same shape. The page: 1228 a failed campaign against the Tavastians, 1230 Michael of Chernigov elected prince, 1233 Novgorodian nobles and allies occupy Izborsk and are expelled by Pskov; none moves the frontier.
Same shape minus two cells in the west (27.3-27.8 E, 57.7-59.0 N); no page dates anything there.

511,500 km2: 140 cells fewer than 1220 in the Ladoga-Onega Karelia (29.9-36.1 E, 59.8-63.3 N); the pages opened give no 1236 event there (the Alexander Nevsky page has only 'In 1236, Alexander was appointed by the Novgorod Republic as the prince of Novgorod'). The shape still holds Pskov, Izborsk and the Votic land (Ingria region), which the pages show Novgorod holding until the Livonian occupation of 1240-1241. Kept; ledger loss at 1236 is confidence 1.

correction.text: the 1236 shape unchanged: Novgorod with Pskov and the Votic land, without the Ladoga-Karelia strip

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Novgorod shape for 1241-1284, but the state goes on (Battle on the Ice 1242, Alexander Nevsky in Novgorod until 1263, the Mongol tribute from 1259). The 1236 shape is used: Pskov, Izborsk and the Votic land were retaken in 1241 ('During the campaign of 1241, Alexander managed to retake both Votia and Pskov'), and Pskov goes in 1285 (split event). Note: Cliopatria's Mongol Empire shape of 1241 covers 835 cells of this land; the pages say only that Novgorod paid tribute from 1259 ('forced it to pay tribute it had previously refused to the Golden Horde'), not that it was conquered.

480,600 km2: the 1236 shape minus 146 cells in the south-west, which are the Pskov land (107 of the 108 cells of Cliopatria's Pskov Republic shape of 1285). Years corrected only: the shape holds 1285-1292 because the Swedish gain of Viborg is dated 1293 (Swedish-Novgorodian Wars page). The Novgorod page has Pskov gaining 'formal independence' only in 1348 (Treaty of Bolotovo); the pskov-republic dossier starts Pskov in 1285 as Cliopatria draws it.

New keyframe, one year: 'In 1293, the Swedes captured part of western Karelia and founded the fortress of Viborg.' Cliopatria's Novgorod loses the corresponding 76 cells (26.7-38.5 E, 60.3-61.9 N) in 1294 and regains 144 cells of Ladoga-Karelia; the 1294 shape is used from 1293.

496,400 km2 for 1294-1313. The page: 1300 the Swedes build Landskrona at the mouth of the Neva, 1301 Novgorod destroys it, 1311 Novgorodians devastate central Finland; none leaves a lasting frontier change.

1,427,900 km2: +3,668 cells (35.7-67.9 E, 56.6-70.4 N): Pomorye, Zavolochye, the Pechora and the Kola side, to the Urals ('At its peak ... extended east to the Urals', Novgorod page; Pomors page: 'In the 12th-15th centuries, Pomorye was considered an extensive colony of' Novgorod). No page dates the extension, so the year is Cliopatria's. Years corrected: this shape holds 1314-1322 because the Treaty of Nöteborg (12 August 1323) moves the Karelian frontier; the Karelian rising of 1314 ended with Karelia again submitting to Novgorod. No Bjarmaland/Dvina area figure exists on the Dvina Land page.

correction.text: the 1326 shape, in force from the Treaty of Nöteborg of 12 August 1323

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1323-1325: Cliopatria draws the post-treaty frontier only from 1326 (+397 cells in eastern Karelia, 28.4-34.8 E, 60.2-66.8 N; -28 cells of Savonian border parishes ceded to Sweden). The page gives 'the Treaty of Nöteborg (12 August 1323)'; the 1326 shape is used from 1323.
1,505,700 km2 for 1326-1332: the post-Nöteborg frontier (see novgorod-republic_1323).
Same shape as 1326; the Novgorod page has no event for 1333.

1,490,300 km2: 69 cells fewer in the south-east (33.4-39.5 E, 56.6-60.2 N), 68 of which Cliopatria gives to the Grand Principality of Moscow in 1344. The Novgorod page says only that 'protracted wars with Moscow over northern lands began' in the late 14th century and dates no 14th-century loss; kept, ledger loss confidence 1.

1,490,400 km2 for 1375-1428. The only dated change on the page is 1397-1398 (see novgorod-republic_1397); 1348 is the Treaty of Bolotovo, in which Pskov gained formal independence (no change to this shape, Pskov being already separate since 1285).

correction.text: the 1375 shape without the Dvina Lands (basin of the Northern Dvina), annexed by Moscow in 1397 and recovered by Novgorod in 1398

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, one year: '1397: Moscow annexed the Dvina Lands; Novgorod recovered them the following year.' The Dvina Land page (a redirect to Bjarmaland) gives only that the territory 'is usually understood to have referred to the southern shores of the White Sea and the basin of the Northern Dvina'; the 200 km band round the river is the researcher's reading.
Same extent (1,490,100 km2); the Novgorod page has Novgorod backing Dmitry Shemyaka in the Muscovite War of Succession 1425-1453 and minting its own denga from 1420, with no frontier change.
Same extent (1,490,800 km2); no page event.

1,461,500 km2: 125 cells fewer round Vologda (38.5-43.2 E, 59.3-61.5 N), all of which Cliopatria adds to Moscow in 1463. The Treaty of Yazhelbitsy page (February 1456) names no cession ('minor territorial concessions' by Vasily II to Novgorod; Novgorod 'deprived of its right to conduct an independent foreign policy'). Kept; ledger loss confidence 1.

1,599,400 km2: +645 cells in the far north (29.0-41.1 E, 65.5-69.5 N), the Kola side. The Pomors page says Pomors explored Kola from a base at Kola and gives no date for Novgorod's rule there; the year is Cliopatria's (ledger gain confidence 1). The infobox of the Novgorod page gives no area.

correction.text: the 1468 shape for 1475-1477 only (Novgorod keeps its whole land until Ivan III takes direct control in January 1478); nothing from 1478

keyframe_review.note: 144,000 km2 (a core of 658 cells, 28.1-36.5 E, 56.4-61.2 N) to 1481, with the 5,900 northern cells given to Moscow from 1475. The Battle of Shelon page: Novgorod 'recognize[d] itself as a patrimony of the grand prince' at Korostyn in 1471 but kept its government; 'he only took direct control of the city-state in January 1478' and 'Novgorod was then formally annexed by Moscow in 1478'. So the full 1468 shape belongs to Novgorod for 1475-1477 and no Novgorod shape exists from 1478.

region.text: Novgorod, given with Kiev to Iziaslav I in Yaroslav's division

ledger.note: 1054: Yaroslav's death divides Rus' and Novgorod goes with Kiev to his eldest son. Kievan Rus' page: 'Principality of Kiev and Novgorod, for the eldest son Iziaslav I of Kiev, who became grand prince', map 'after the death of Yaroslav I in 1054'; the Yaroslav the Wise page infobox gives his death on 20 February 1054. Cliopatria's Novgorod shape begins in 1056.

region.text: the Vaga-Sukhona-Dvina side of the portage added to the Novgorod shape in 1126 (+693 cells)

ledger.note: 1126: the Novgorod land reaches the portage and the Dvina side (Cliopatria). The pages give no year: Pomors page 'As early as the 12th century, explorers from Novgorod entered the White Sea through the Northern Dvina' and 'In the 12th-15th centuries, Pomorye was considered an extensive colony of' Novgorod; Novgorod page 1079 'beyond the portage'. Year is Cliopatria's.

1136: Novgorod throws off the princes of Kiev and becomes a republic. Page infobox 'Established 1136'; the Novgorodians 'deposed Vsevolod Mstislavich and began electing and dismissing princes'; Kievan Rus' page: 'In 1136, Novgorod revolted against Kiev, and became independent.' Colour and dossier continue (rule 2).

region.text: the Ladoga-Onega Karelia strip (140 cells) missing from the Novgorod shape of 1236-1284

ledger.note: 1236: Cliopatria's Novgorod loses the Ladoga-Onega Karelia strip. No page dates it: the Alexander Nevsky page has only that Alexander became prince of Novgorod in 1236; the Karelians dossier (karelians) draws the Karelian land as its own from 1143. Year and counterpart are Cliopatria's reading.

region.text: Izborsk and Pskov

ledger.note: September 1240: Izborsk and Pskov fall to the Livonian side. Battle on the Ice page: Yaroslav of Pskov 'failed in 1233, but succeeded during the September 1240 Izborsk and Pskov campaign', helped by bishop Hermann of Dorpat; the infobox lists 'Livonian troops withdrawn'. The occupier is read as the Livonian Order (a branch of the Teutonic Order, the successor of the Brothers of the Sword), the page naming no single power.

region.text: Votia (the Votic land), a Novgorodian tributary

ledger.note: Winter 1240-1241: the Votic land is overrun. Battle on the Ice page: 'in the winter of 1240-1241, the combined forces of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek' launched the Votia campaign (Votia, a Novgorodian tributary, per the Novgorod page). The page gives no month; December marks the start of the winter. The Bishopric has no Cliopatria row; its dossier is bishopric-of-osel-wiek.

region.text: Izborsk and Pskov

ledger.note: 1241: Alexander Nevsky retakes Pskov. 'During the campaign of 1241, Alexander managed to retake both Votia and Pskov'; Alexander Nevsky page: 'conquered Pskov and Koporye from the crusaders'. The Battle on the Ice (5 April 1242) then 'prevented the crusaders from retaking Pskov'.

region.text: Votia (the Votic land)

ledger.note: 1241: Votia and the fortress of Koporye are retaken. Footnote: 'Having conquered the fortress and captured the remaining Latin Christians'; the peace of 1242 has the Order abandon 'the land of the Vod people, of Luga, Pleskov [Pskov], and Lotygola [Latgale]'.

region.text: the Pskov land, 107 of whose 108 cells lie in Novgorod's 1236 shape

ledger.note: 1285: Pskov stands apart from Novgorod (Cliopatria's Pskov Republic row begins). Novgorod page: Pskov 'gained formal independence under the Treaty of Bolotovo (1348)', so the page makes Pskov a dependency of Novgorod until 1348; the pskov-republic dossier starts Pskov in 1285 and records Bolotovo as a rename. Year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: western Karelia round Viborg and the north-west Ladoga shore, lost from the shape in 1294 (76 cells)

ledger.note: 1293: the Swedes take part of western Karelia and found Viborg. 'In 1293, the Swedes captured part of western Karelia and founded the fortress of Viborg.' The page does not say the land was Novgorod's; Cliopatria's shape loses 76 cells there in 1294 and the kingdom-of-sweden dossier records the matching gain.

region.text: the Ladoga-Karelia strip back in the Novgorod shape (144 cells)

ledger.note: 1294: Cliopatria's Novgorod regains the Ladoga-Karelia strip it lacked since 1236 (+144 cells). The Swedish-Novgorodian Wars page has no 1294 event; the Karelians dossier has Novgorod fighting the Karelians from 1278 (not on the page opened).

region.text: the mouth of the Neva and the Okhta, where Landskrona stood

ledger.note: 1300: the Swedes build Landskrona at the mouth of the Neva. 'Seven years later [after Viborg, 1293], they established the fortress of Landskrona at the mouth of the Neva' on the Okhta, destroying Novgorodian settlements there.

region.text: the mouth of the Neva and the Okhta, where Landskrona stood

ledger.note: 1301: Novgorod destroys Landskrona. 'Later that year, Novgorodian troops counterattacked and destroyed Landskrona.'

region.text: Karelia

ledger.note: 1314: Karelia rises against Novgorod. 'Three years later [after 1311], dissatisfaction with Novgorodian rule erupted in Karelia.'

region.text: Karelia

ledger.note: 1314: the rising is put down after several months. 'After several months, Karelia again submitted to Novgorod's authority.'

region.text: the north from the White Sea coast to the Urals and the Arctic coast (3,668 cells, 35.7-67.9 E)

ledger.note: 1314: the Novgorod shape swells over the whole north (Cliopatria): Pomorye, Zavolochye, the Pechora and the Urals side, +3,668 cells. No page dates it: Pomors page 'In the 12th-15th centuries, Pomorye was considered an extensive colony of' Novgorod; Novgorod page: at its peak it 'extended east to the Urals'. The Dvina Land page adds that the Bjarmians 'became tributaries of the Novgorod Republic' after their 13th-century decline. Year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the Savonian border parishes ceded to Sweden (28 cells, 28.8-29.9 E, 60.3-62.1 N)

ledger.note: 12 August 1323: the Treaty of Nöteborg gives Sweden the border parishes of Savonia. 'The Treaty of Nöteborg (12 August 1323)' ended the war; the kingdom-of-sweden dossier names the pogosts of Savilahti (Mikkeli), Jääski and Äyräpää. The page itself does not list them; Cliopatria's shape loses 28 cells there in 1326.

region.text: eastern Karelia, the north and west Onega-Ladoga side (397 cells, 28.4-34.8 E, 60.2-66.8 N)

ledger.note: 12 August 1323: eastern Karelia goes to Novgorod under the Treaty of Nöteborg. The page dates the treaty and has Karelia under Novgorod's authority after 1314; Cliopatria adds the Ladoga-Onega Karelia (+397 cells) in 1326, which the karelians dossier records as 'eastern Karelia goes to Novgorod' in 1323.

region.text: the south-east strip (33.4-39.5 E, 56.6-60.2 N, 69 cells)

ledger.note: 1344: Moscow's shape takes cells in the Volga-Mologa south-east of the Novgorod land (Cliopatria; 68 of the 69 cells Novgorod loses). The Novgorod page dates no 14th-century cession ('Late 14th century: Protracted wars with Moscow over northern lands began'). Year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the Dvina Lands, the basin of the Northern Dvina

ledger.note: 1397: Moscow annexes the Dvina Lands. '1397: Moscow annexed the Dvina Lands; Novgorod recovered them the following year.' Cliopatria shows no change.

region.text: the Dvina Lands, the basin of the Northern Dvina

ledger.note: 1398: Novgorod recovers the Dvina Lands, 'the following year'.

region.text: the Vologda side (38.5-43.2 E, 59.3-61.5 N, 125 cells)

ledger.note: 1463: Moscow's shape takes the Vologda side of the Novgorod land (125 cells, all in Cliopatria's Moscow gain of 1463). No page opened dates it; the Treaty of Yazhelbitsy page (February 1456) names no territory. Year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the Kola and Murman side (29.0-41.1 E, 65.5-69.5 N)

ledger.note: 1468: Cliopatria's Novgorod shape reaches the Kola coast (+645 cells). The Pomors page has Pomors exploring Kola from a base at Kola and dates no Novgorod rule there. Year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the Novgorod heartland round Lake Ilmen and the Shelon River, where the armies met (the left bank of the Shelon on 14 July)

ledger.note: 23 May 1471: Ivan III goes to war with Novgorod. 'On 23 May 1471, Ivan III went to war with Novgorod'; the Novgorodians had invited the Lithuanian prince Mikhailo Olelkovich in 1470.

region.text: the Novgorod heartland round Lake Ilmen and the Shelon River

ledger.note: 14 July 1471: Moscow wins at the Shelon and Novgorod then signs the Treaty of Korostyn. 'The battle took place on the morning of 14 July on the left bank of the Shelon River'; 'Novgorod signed the Treaty of Korostyn, which required it to recognize itself as a patrimony of the grand prince' and barred it from inviting Lithuanian princes. The month is that of the battle, the last fighting; the page gives no date for the treaty.

region.text: the whole Novgorod land

ledger.note: January 1478: Ivan III annexes Novgorod. 'he only took direct control of the city-state in January 1478'; 'Novgorod was then formally annexed by Moscow in 1478' (the Novgorod page: he 'abolished the veche').

region.text: the whole Novgorod land

ledger.note: January 1478: the Novgorod Republic ends. Infobox 'disestablished 1478'; Ivan III 'abolished the veche, and took more than four-fifths of the land'. The land passes to the Grand Principality of Moscow.

wars.name: Battle on the Ice
wars.outcome: Novgorod-Vladimir victory: Pskov, Votia and Koporye retaken in 1241, the Order beaten on Lake Peipus on 5 April 1242 and, in the settlement, giving up 'the land of the Vod people, of Luga, Pleskov [Pskov], and Lotygola [Latgale]'.
wars.note: Infobox territorial changes: 'Peace agreed, prisoners exchanged, Livonian troops withdrawn'. The page notes that the 1240 Battle of the Neva (15 July, Alexander Nevsky page) is attested only in Rus' sources.

wars.name: Swedish–Novgorodian Wars

zones.text: western Karelia and the Karelian Isthmus

wars.outcome: Mixed: Novgorod holds the Neva (Landskrona destroyed 1301), Sweden takes Viborg (1293); the Treaty of Nöteborg (12 August 1323) fixes the frontier; Magnus Eriksson's 1348 crusade burns Oreshek and Novgorod regains control; last recorded conflict 1445.
wars.note: Dates from the page: 1240 Neva (July), 1256 Novgorodian raid on Swedish Finland, 1293 Viborg, 1300-1301 Landskrona, 1311 Häme War, 1314 Karelian rising, 1323 treaty, 1348-1351 'Disputed'.

wars.name: Karelian rising of 1314
wars.outcome: Karelia 'again submitted to Novgorod's authority' after several months.

wars.name: Treaty of Yazhelbitsy
wars.outcome: Novgorod 'sustained a crushing defeat' in 1456 and signed at Yazhelbitsy in February 1456, losing its independent foreign policy and legislation; no territory is named on the page.
wars.note: Cliopatria's 1463 loss of the Vologda side is not tied to this treaty by the page.

wars.name: Battle of Shelon

zones.text: the Novgorod heartland round Lake Ilmen and the Shelon River

wars.outcome: Moscow wins at the Shelon on 14 July 1471 (Novgorodians at least 10,000 against 4,000-5,000); the Treaty of Korostyn makes Novgorod 'a patrimony of the grand prince' and bars Lithuanian princes. No territory is named.
wars.note: Background: Novgorod's treaty with Casimir IV of Lithuania 'was likely not approved by Casimir IV' (grand-duchy-of-lithuania was not a belligerent on the page); Mikhailo Olelkovich was invited in 1470, arrived in November and left four months later.

wars.name: Annexation of Novgorod by Moscow
wars.outcome: Ivan III marches in the winter of 1477-1478, takes direct control in January 1478 and abolishes the veche; Novgorod is 'formally annexed by Moscow in 1478'.

certainty.note: Forest, lake and portage frontiers never fixed by treaty; the western frontier with the Livonian Order is settled in the peace of 1242 only by naming lands, not a line.

The Swedish frontier on the Karelian Isthmus and in Savonia is regulated by the Treaty of Nöteborg (12 August 1323) and is the one sharper border; the northern colonies (Pomorye, Zavolochye, Pechora, Kola) are soft throughout.

notes:
Start: the page (infobox) gives 1136 for the republic and Cliopatria draws a Novgorod shape from 1056; this dossier starts in 1054 (Yaroslav's division, 20 February 1054, which the rus dossier already uses as its end) and records 1136 as a rename. A new keyframe covers 1054-1055. The Novgorod page's native-name and ruler lists are partial (no full prince list), so identity.rulers is omitted.

Page budget: 9 pages (Novgorod Republic, Dvina Land which is a redirect to Bjarmaland, Swedish-Novgorodian Wars, Battle of Shelon, Pomors, Battle on the Ice, Treaty of Yazhelbitsy, Alexander Nevsky, Kievan Rus' shared with the other four dossiers) plus the Yaroslav the Wise page (shared, for the 20 February 1054 date). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zavolochye failed (url_not_found); the Pomors page is silent on Zavolochye, Yugra, Perm and the Dvina Land, so the north rests on Cliopatria's 1126, 1314 and 1468 steps at confidence 1.

Unsettled, in order of weight:
1. The north (1126 +163,000 km2; 1314 +3,668 cells; 1468 +645 cells; 1344 and 1463 losses to Moscow): all four years are Cliopatria's; no page opened dates a Novgorod acquisition of Pomorye, Zavolochye, the Pechora, Kola or Perm, or the 1344/1463 losses. A gap-filler should open the Wikipedia pages of Zavolochye (try 'Zavolochie'), Great Perm, Yugra, Kola and the Muscovite-Novgorodian wars.
2. 1475-1481: Cliopatria's Novgorod core to 1481 and Moscow's northern shape from 1475 contradict the pages (annexation January 1478; Korostyn 1471 makes Novgorod 'a patrimony of the grand prince' without taking land). The 1475 shape is marked wrong for 1478-1481 and corrected to the 1468 shape for 1475-1477. The grand-principality-of-moscow dossier (eu-16-g, not yet on disk when this was written) should start the northern land in 1478 and carry a vassal_start for Novgorod at the 1471 Korostyn treaty.
3. Pskov: the page makes Pskov formally independent only in 1348 (Treaty of Bolotovo); Cliopatria separates Pskov in 1285; the ledger follows Cliopatria (split 1285, confidence 1) and the pskov-republic dossier (eu-16-e) agrees.
4. Karelia: the karelians dossier draws Karelian land as a separate state from 1143 to 1322, which overlaps Cliopatria's Novgorod shape 1143-1235 (553 of the Karelia region's 955 cells) and 1294-1322; the Swedish-Novgorodian Wars page has Karelia under Novgorod's authority in 1314. The 1236 loss and 1294 gain (confidence 1) are Cliopatria's.
5. The Mongol Empire's Cliopatria shape of 1241 covers 835 of the Novgorod 1285 cells; the Alexander Nevsky page has Novgorod paying tribute to the Golden Horde from 1259, not conquest. The mongol-empire dossier's vassal_start for Novgorod in 1241 (confidence from Cliopatria) is two decades earlier than the page.
6. Counterparts with no dossier: Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek (1240-1241 occupation of Votia; no Cliopatria row), grand-principality-of-moscow (not yet written when this was done; named by slug), teutonic-order is used for the Livonian Order (the Livonian Brothers of the Sword had merged in 1237).

Not on a page opened and so not in the ledger: Novgorod's 1259 submission to Mongol tribute (Alexander Nevsky page: 'forced it to pay tribute it had previously refused to the Golden Horde' is a vassal relation for the mongol-empire/golden-horde dossier), the 1348-1349 Swedish occupation of Oreshek (the page says only that the king 'set it ablaze, but Novgorod soon regained control'; the kingdom-of-sweden dossier has it as an occupation), the Lithuanian frontier (Velikiye Luki and Toropets).
